cards.title: Purified versus discrete quantum access for classical distribution testing
cards.formal: Do purified quantum access and discrete quantum query access give equivalent query complexity for classical distributional property-testing problems, in the source’s regime where the discrete seed set is much larger than the outcome alphabet? The missing direction is to show that discrete access gives no asymptotic testing advantage over purified access. Discrete access can already realize purified access with constant overhead. The source leaves the comparison’s overhead and the precise large-seed-space regime implicit, so this is a recovered equivalence conjecture whose parameter conventions still need specification.
cards.why: Would establish whether quantum distribution-testing complexity is robust to two common ways of exposing a sampling procedure, and allow matching upper and lower bounds to be compared on a common basis.
cards.status_note: Read the source’s complete question and oracle definitions, Belovs’s model relations and two-distribution theorem, and the later entropy preprint’s treatment of the conjecture. Searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate a general resolution. The source’s equivalence overhead and common-domain/seed-size regime remain insufficiently specified.

progress.text: Belovs compares four interfaces, proves special-case and one-way results, and conjectures the general equivalence.

cards.review_note: The source does not quantify the large seed-space regime |S|≫n relative to testing accuracy and query budget, or the allowed overhead meant by equivalent. Exact discrete access only represents probabilities on a denominator-|S| grid, so a comparison with arbitrary real distributions needs a common-domain or approximation convention. The precise class of testing promises and the treatment of controlled queries and ancillary-register size must accompany that comparison. These choices are not silently replaced by a constant-factor theorem on an arbitrarily chosen grid.

importance.reason: A broad robustness question for quantum access to classical distributions and the interpretation of property-testing bounds. Existing score retained.

sentences: Quantum testers can access a distribution either through a reversible sampler with an ancillary register or through queries to a finite list of outcome labels.
The conjecture asks whether these two interfaces have the same power for classical distribution testing when the list is sufficiently large.
The list interface already implements purified access with constant query overhead.
Known two-distribution results and entropy algorithms do not prove the missing general direction.
The acceptable overhead and the relation among list length, accuracy and the represented distributions still need to be fixed.

cards.definitions: A classical distribution is p=(p₁,…,pₙ), with pᵢ≥0 and Σᵢpᵢ=1 on outcomes [n]={1,…,n}. Purified access supplies a unitary Uₚ and its inverse Uₚ† such that Uₚ|0⟩A|0⟩B=Σᵢ√pᵢ|φᵢ⟩A|i⟩B, where the states |φᵢ⟩ are orthonormal. Ignoring A leaves the diagonal density matrix Σᵢpᵢ|i⟩⟨i|, and measuring B samples p. The ancillary states are not supplied as known classical descriptions. An algorithm must work for the valid encodings of p, including arbitrary unitary actions away from the designated all-zero input; the oracle matrix is not given explicitly. Discrete access instead gives a finite seed set S=[N] and quantum value queries to f:S→[n] with pᵢ=|f⁻¹(i)|/N. A clean value query maps |s,0⟩ to |s,f(s)⟩ reversibly, with inverse access; a usual full implementation XORs the fixed binary encoding of f(s) into the target register. The ordering of seeds is not part of the property being tested. The integers n,N describe input spaces, and the values of f are available only through queries. Each forward or inverse oracle invocation costs one; superposition of seed values is allowed, and non-oracle quantum computation is not counted as queries. A distribution-testing task specifies accepting and rejecting promises on distributions, and a tester must give the corresponding answer with bounded error on each promised distribution. In ordinary ε-property testing the promises are p∈P versus inf_{q∈P} (1/2)Σᵢ|pᵢ−qᵢ|≥ε; tasks comparing more than one unknown distribution additionally require access to each. The source asks about distributional testing generally, rather than fixing only this example. Error such as 1/3 is over the algorithm’s measurement and random outcomes, with oracle encodings treated in the worst case. Purified access is distinct from pure-state preparation |0⟩↦Σᵢ√pᵢ|i⟩ with no garbage register, which is a stronger input model. Exact discrete access restricts p to multiples of 1/N; purified access has no such rationality restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: For a fully specified common class of testing tasks, distributions and parameter regimes, prove matching query complexities with the stipulated overhead in both models, or give a task with a separation exceeding that overhead in the same regime. The unknown direction would bound purified-access complexity in terms of discrete-access complexity. A simulation in the already-known direction, a tester for just one property, or a separation involving the stronger pure-state model does not settle the general conjecture. The current source leaves the comparison scale and denominator/accuracy conventions incomplete.

context_blocks.title: The established direction must not be reversed
context_blocks.text: A uniform superposition of seeds followed by one value query prepares a purification of the frequency distribution. Thus a tester designed for purified access can be run from discrete access. This transfers purified-model upper bounds to discrete access, and discrete-model lower bounds to purified access.

context_blocks.title: The garbage register affects the available information
context_blocks.text: Removing the ancillary register from the access promise changes the model. Belovs separates pure-state preparation from the more general distribution interfaces, so the word purified cannot be replaced by an amplitude vector alone.

context_blocks.title: Two hypotheses are a solved special case
context_blocks.text: Belovs determines the query complexity of distinguishing two fully specified distributions in terms of their Hellinger distance across the models. He also relates frequency encodings and randomly sampled lists below a seed-length-dependent query scale. His conclusion still leaves the general discrete-versus-purified equivalence conjectural.

context_blocks.title: Later shared upper bounds use the known direction
context_blocks.text: The 2021 entropy preprint explicitly repeats the equivalence conjecture while explaining that its purified-access algorithms apply in the other models. That transfer alone does not prove equality of optimal complexities for every testing problem.

cards.context:
A uniform superposition of seeds followed by one value query prepares a purification of the frequency distribution. Thus a tester designed for purified access can be run from discrete access. This transfers purified-model upper bounds to discrete access, and discrete-model lower bounds to purified access.

Removing the ancillary register from the access promise changes the model. Belovs separates pure-state preparation from the more general distribution interfaces, so the word purified cannot be replaced by an amplitude vector alone.

Belovs determines the query complexity of distinguishing two fully specified distributions in terms of their Hellinger distance across the models. He also relates frequency encodings and randomly sampled lists below a seed-length-dependent query scale. His conclusion still leaves the general discrete-versus-purified equivalence conjectural.

The 2021 entropy preprint explicitly repeats the equivalence conjecture while explaining that its purified-access algorithms apply in the other models. That transfer alone does not prove equality of optimal complexities for every testing problem.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
